{{Short description|Type of spline in applied mathematics}}
In [[applied mathematics]], an '''Akima spline''' is a type of non-smoothing [[Spline (mathematics)|spline]] that gives good fits to curves where the second derivative is rapidly varying.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.alglib.net/interpolation/spline3.php#header5|title=Spline interpolation and fitting – ALGLIB, C++ and C# library|website=www.alglib.net}}</ref> The Akima spline was published by Hiroshi Akima in 1970 from Akima's pursuit of a [[Spline (mathematics)|cubic spline]] curve that would appear more natural and smooth, akin to an intuitively hand-drawn curve.<ref name="Akima1970" /><ref name=":0">{{Citation |last=Salomon |first=David |chapter=Raster Graphics |date=2011 |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/978-0-85729-886-7_2 |title=Texts in Computer Science |pages=29–134 |access-date=2023-10-23 |place=London |publisher=Springer London |isbn=978-0-85729-885-0}}</ref> The Akima spline has become the algorithm of choice for several computer graphics applications.<ref name=":0" /> Its advantage over the cubic spline curve is its stability with respect to outliers.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Siddiqi, Al-Lawati, Boulbrachene |first=Abul Hasan, Mohamed, Messaoud |title=Modern Engineering Mathematics |publisher=CRC |year=2017 |isbn=9781498712095}}</ref>

==Method==
Given a set of "knot" points <math>(x_i, y_i)_{i=1\dots n}</math>, where the <math>x_i</math> are strictly increasing, the Akima spline will go through each of the given points.  At those points, its slope, <math>s_i</math>, is a function of the locations of the points <math>(x_{i-2}, y_{i-2})</math> through <math>(x_{i+2}, y_{i+2})</math>.  Specifically, if we define <math>m_i</math> as the slope of the [[line segment]] from <math>(x_i, y_i)</math> to <math>(x_{i+1},y_{i+1})</math>, namely
:<math>m_i=\frac{y_{i+1} - y_i}{x_{i+1}-x_i} \,,</math>
then the spline slopes <math>s_i</math> are defined as the following
[[weighted arithmetic mean|weighted average]] of <math>m_{i-1}</math> and <math>m_i</math>,

:<math>s_i = \frac{|m_{i+1} - m_i|m_{i-1} + |m_{i-1} - m_{i-2}|m_i}{|m_{i+1} - m_i| + |m_{i-1} - m_{i-2}|} \,.</math>

If the denominator equals zero, the slope is given as

:<math>s_i=\frac{m_{i-1}+m_{i}}{2}\,.</math>

The first two and the last two points need a special prescription, for example,

:<math>s_1=m_1 \,, s_2=\frac{m_{1}+m_{2}}{2} \,, s_{n-1}=\frac{m_{n-2}+m_{n-1}}{2} \,, s_n=m_{n-1} \,.</math>

The spline is then defined as the [[piecewise]] [[cubic function]] whose value between <math>x_i</math> and <math>x_{i+1}</math> is the unique cubic polynomial <math>P_i(x)</math>,

:<math>P_i(x)=a_i+b_i(x-x_i)+c_i(x-x_i)^2+d_i(x-x_i)^3 \,,</math>

where the coefficients of the polynomial are chosen such that the four conditions of continuity of the spline together with its first derivative are satisfied,

:<math>P(x_i) = y_i \,,  P(x_{i+1}) = y_{i+1} \,,  P'(x_i) = s_i \,,  P'(x_{i+1}) = s_{i+1} \,.</math>

which gives

:<math>a_i=y_i \,,</math>
:<math>b_i=s_i \,,</math>
:<math>c_i=\frac{3m_i-2s_i-s_{i+1}}{x_{i+1}-x_i} \,,</math>
:<math>d_i=\frac{s_i+s_{i+1}-2m_i}{(x_{i+1}-x_i)^2} \,.</math>

Due to these conditions the Akima spline is a &nbsp;C<sup>1</sup> [[differentiable function]], that is, the function itself is continuous and the first derivative is also continuous. However, in general, the second derivative is not necessarily continuous.

An advantage of the Akima spline is due to the fact that it uses only values from neighboring knot points in the construction of the coefficients of the interpolation polynomial between any two knot points. This means that there is no large system of equations to solve and the Akima spline avoids unphysical wiggles in regions where the second derivative in the underlying curve is rapidly changing. A possible disadvantage of the Akima spline is that it has a discontinuous second derivative.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.iue.tuwien.ac.at/phd/rottinger/node60.html|title=The Akima Interpolation}}</ref>
